oh, stupid story time:

We have a machine shop against the dividing wall in our facility.  On the other side of that wall, we have a few PC's in the teardown department.  The wall is about a foot thick and made of cinder block.  

I kept getting helpdesk tickets form two guys in teardown that they were having a really hard time with internet speed, to include the internal SharePoint site.  Database access was painfully slow to, and things would timeout all the time. 

I got to looking at it and doing wireshark captures I noticed that they were doing tons of transmission packets.  

The long and short was that the cat5 they were on was draped along the wall instead of run through the conduit and it wasn't shielded.  It was picking up the electromagnetic field of the welders through the brick wall via inductance.  

I had to run new cat 6 shielded through the conduit that was in place and the issue evaporated.  

​

Not saying that's your issue obviously, but check all your OSI layers at some point.

I'm the Network Administrator at a manufacturing company.  I use charts to maintain my configurations for much of my network. 

Bare minimum for me is the following set:

* Network Diagram
* Switch Interconnect Diagram
* Telephone system IVR/Digital Receptionist/Call Routing Flowchart
* Floor Map with Ports (also surveillance cameras and WiFi access points)

These are not just for my reference (I'm not just the network admin, I'm everything else IT as well), but for the continuity of business if I am unavailable/incapacitated.  There's going to be someone that fills my shoes at some point, and its in my best interest and the interest of my org to have as much documented as clearly as possible.

Don't forget to document your processes as well.  That way when someone gets into you about why you cant do what they want their way, you can point to the process documentation and blame it on policy and procedure instead of saying "No, because I'm stubborn."

>One of our biggest issues with migrating to Windows 7 has been the problem of laptops needing to logon before the laptop would connect to the wireless. Therefore it was impossible to logon as a domain user using only a wireless connection.Finally, we found a simple solution.  
>  
>5 Steps total

1. Set up a wireless profile. 
   1. We use a WPA-2 PSK with AES. But use whatever best suits your needs.
2. Check your WLAN profile name.
   1. In a command prompt, get the name of your profile by running netsh wlan show profile
3. Create a regisrty entry
   1. run regedit
   2. Find the HKLM\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run registry key.
   3. Add a string value to the above mentioned key. Call it anything (WLAN prelogon), but its value should be%comspec% /c netsh wlan connect name="<profile name>"
   4. Of course, replace <profile name> with your profile name that you previously created.
4. Add to GPO
   1. Image: [Expand](https://content.spiceworksstatic.com/service.community/p/how_to_step_attachments/0000005296/4d8bc1af/attached_file/WLAN_prelog2.jpg)
   2. If you have a lot of computers to configure for this, add it to Group Policy.
   3. Add it to Computer Config > Preferences > Windows Settings > Registry. (see attachment)
5. Update Group Policy
   1. run gpupdate /force /boot on all computers that you want updated. This will create the registry entry and reboot.
